lead: FM gives a large noise improvement only while the received carrier is well above the noise. Below an input carrier-to-noise ratio of about 10 dB the detector output breaks into jumps and clicks, and the output SNR falls far faster than the ideal law predicts. This is the threshold effect. The same nonlinear detector behaviour gives the capture effect: of two co-channel FM signals, the stronger one takes over the detector output and the weaker is effectively rejected, provided the stronger exceeds it by the capture ratio, typically a few dB. Threshold and capture decide FM broadcast quality and co-channel reuse.
prereq: You need Chapter 3.5 for the above-threshold output SNR law, and Unit 1 for noise power in a bandwidth.

blocks.text: FM noise performance has two regimes. In the good regime the carrier is much larger than the noise in the IF bandwidth. CNR means carrier power divided by noise power in that bandwidth. The limiter removes amplitude noise, and the discriminator output noise is small. The output SNR then follows a straight-line law: every extra dB of input CNR gives one extra dB of output SNR, plus a fixed FM improvement set by the modulation index.

blocks.where: (S/N)<sub>out</sub> is output signal-to-noise ratio in dB; (C/N)<sub>in</sub> is input carrier-to-noise ratio in dB; I<sub>FM</sub> is the FM improvement in dB, fixed by the modulation index and bandwidth.

blocks.text: Below about 10 dB input CNR the carrier no longer dominates. For short intervals noise exceeds the carrier. The limiter follows the noise, the estimated instantaneous frequency jumps, and the discriminator output shows spikes called clicks. A click is a large error, not a small one. The output SNR now falls steeply, much faster than linearly. This collapse is the threshold effect.

Define the threshold as the input CNR at which the output SNR is 1 dB below the above-threshold law. Practical receivers put this knee near 10 dB. Threshold is a property of the input CNR, not of the output SNR. A receiver with a higher modulation index has a better above-threshold law but usually a higher threshold.

sections.h3: The two-region curve and threshold extension

blocks.text: The figure plots output SNR against input CNR. The straight line is the above-threshold law; here it is x + 15.7 dB. The measured points sit on the line at 12 dB input and above, where the actual output is 27.7 dB. At 10 dB input the actual output is already about 20 dB, roughly 6 dB below the ideal 25.7 dB, so this receiver's 1 dB threshold lies near 11–12 dB. At 8 dB input the ideal line would give 23.7 dB, but the actual output is only about 6 dB. The curve has a sharp knee, which is why engineers speak of an FM threshold.

Threshold extension methods move the knee to lower input CNR. An FM feedback loop (FMFB) uses a narrow IF filter that follows the instantaneous carrier, so less noise enters. A phase-locked loop (PLL) detector tracks carrier phase and does not produce the same click spikes. Only a few universities teach these methods in detail. Know the names, the aim, and that they trade complexity for a lower threshold.

Capture effect appears when two FM signals share one channel. The receiver limiter sees the sum. If one signal is stronger by more than the capture ratio, the discriminator output follows only the stronger signal; the weaker is suppressed. Capture ratio is the minimum input power ratio, in dB, of the stronger to the weaker signal for the stronger to win. It is typically a few dB.

This helps FM broadcasting. A distant co-channel station is weaker at your receiver, so it is captured out and you hear only the local station, with less co-channel interference than AM would give. It also helps cellular reuse. The same channel can be reused in another cell if the local base station is stronger than the distant co-channel base station by the capture ratio. If the interferer becomes stronger, the receiver captures the wrong signal. Capture ratio is a two-signal specification; threshold is a signal-to-noise specification.

figure.caption: The straight line is the above-threshold FM law; the measured curve sits on it down to about 12 dB input CNR, is already about 6 dB low at 10 dB, and drops sharply below that. This receiver's 1 dB threshold is near 11–12 dB.

spec.aria: The straight line is the ideal above-threshold FM law; the measured curve sits on it down to about 12 dB input CNR, is about 6 dB low at 10 dB, and drops sharply below that. This receiver's 1 dB threshold is near 11–12 dB.

examples.question: An FM receiver has an IF bandwidth B = 180 kHz, a noise figure F = 1 (0 dB), and an antenna temperature T0 = 290 K. Use kT0 = 4 × 10⁻²¹ W/Hz. The threshold is taken as an input CNR of 10 dB. Find the input noise power in W and dBm, and the input carrier power at threshold in W and dBm.
steps: Noise power N = kT0B = (4 × 10⁻²¹ W/Hz)(1.8 × 10⁵ Hz) = 7.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ W.
Convert N to dBm: N(dBm) = 10 log₁₀(N / 1 × 10⁻³ W) = 10 log₁₀(7.2 × 10⁻¹³) = −121.4 dBm.
At threshold CNR = 10 dB, which is a power ratio of 10. Carrier power C = 10 × N = 10 × 7.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ W = 7.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ W.
Convert C to dBm: C(dBm) = −121.4 dBm + 10 dB = −111.4 dBm.
examples.answer: Noise power N = 7.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ W = −121.4 dBm; input carrier power at threshold C = 7.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ W = −111.4 dBm.

import math
k = 4e-21
B = 180e3
N = k * B
N_dBm = 10 * math.log10(N / 1e-3)
C = 10 * N
C_dBm = 10 * math.log10(C / 1e-3)
print(f"{N:.1e}")
print(f"{N_dBm:.1f}")
print(f"{C:.1e}")
print(f"{C_dBm:.1f}")

traps: The threshold is an input CNR of about 10 dB; do not quote it as an output SNR or as a fixed carrier power in watts.
Below threshold the output SNR does not follow the above-threshold line; do not use (S/N)out = (C/N)in + IFM there.
Capture ratio is not threshold. Capture ratio compares two co-channel signal powers; threshold compares carrier with noise.
A larger modulation index improves the above-threshold output SNR but raises the threshold; do not claim it always improves reception.
Noise figure 0 dB means F = 1, not zero noise; antenna noise kT0B still exists.

quiz.a: The input CNR at which the output SNR is 1 dB below the above-threshold straight-line law; about 10 dB in practical receivers.

quiz.q: Why does the output SNR fall faster than the input CNR below threshold?
quiz.a: Noise momentarily exceeds the carrier, the limiter follows noise, the instantaneous frequency estimate jumps, and the discriminator produces large click spikes. Each click adds a large error, so output SNR drops steeply.

quiz.q: An FM receiver follows (S/N)out = (C/N)in + 14 dB above threshold. Find output SNR for input CNR 24 dB. If input CNR falls to 8 dB, can you use this formula?
quiz.a: At 24 dB output = 24 + 14 = 38 dB. At 8 dB the formula is invalid because it is below threshold; actual output is much lower.

quiz.q: Two co-channel FM signals arrive at −70 dBm and −75 dBm. Capture ratio is 3 dB. Which signal does the receiver follow?
quiz.a: Difference = 5 dB > 3 dB, so the −70 dBm signal captures the receiver.

quiz.q: Why is capture effect useful for FM broadcasting and for cellular reuse?
quiz.a: A weaker co-channel station is suppressed, reducing interference; the same channel can be reused if the local signal exceeds the co-channel signal by the capture ratio, but if the interferer is stronger the receiver captures the wrong signal.

quiz.q: Is capture ratio the same as threshold? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Threshold is input CNR for a 1 dB drop in output SNR. Capture ratio is input power ratio of two co-channel signals for the stronger to suppress the weaker.

quiz.q: An FM IF bandwidth is 200 kHz and kT0 = 4 × 10⁻²¹ W/Hz. Find the noise power.

beyond: Not for the exam. FM threshold extension appears in satellite and deep-space receivers, where every dB of carrier power is expensive. Click-noise analysis is still used to predict FM link outages. Capture effect underlies co-channel reuse planning in analog cellular systems. Search for FM threshold extension, click noise in FM, and capture ratio.
